text: Good evening. I'm Meena Krishnan. I teach English at Lincoln Middle, and I run the youth program at {homeCenter}, and these days most of the rest of it. $ This month two of my students stayed home for a week because their parents heard about checks near the bus depot. Their classmates noticed. Kids notice everything. The rules coming out of Washington are teaching our children that there are two kinds of families in this town: the ones who can walk to school and the ones who can't. That is divisive, and I don't think it's an accident. $ I'd like the next governor to say out loud that every child in this state belongs in a classroom, and then put money behind it.

You asked what the state can actually do. Three things, and none of them is expensive. Interpreters at every parent night, so a twelve-year-old isn't translating his own report card. A rule, in writing, that schools and clinics don't hand out addresses. And money for the places where people meet across the lines: the library's homework club, our lantern night, the cricket field the doctors share with a softball team. $ Fear makes people stay with their own. I understand that; I feel it too. But the families getting through this month are the ones who know a neighbour on the other side. I've watched it happen. Give us more of those neighbours.

Good evening. I'm Meena Krishnan. I teach English at Lincoln Middle, and I run the youth program at {homeCenter}, and these days most of the rest of it. $ I'll start with something good, because it's been a while. This fall the district started booking interpreters for parent nights, in whatever language a family asks for. Last week a father who had never come to a conference sat across from his daughter's teacher and asked about her maths, in his own language. She sat next to him and didn't translate a word. $ That's what the president's direction looks like at one small table. I'm glad. A country that counts everybody's parents is the one I want my students to grow up in. Keep the state moving that way.

You asked whether the state should fund centers like ours. Yes, with one condition I'd write myself: open some of the doors. Our hall has a kitchen, a stage and two hundred folding chairs. On a Monday it could be a flu clinic. On a Thursday, a homework club for any kid on Grand Avenue. The library already lends us tables; we can lend back. $ Some people at the hall worry that the money comes with strings. Sometimes it does, and we should read every page. But I'd rather our kids grow up as the experts at a mixed table than as guests at nobody's. Fund the places where people cross over. That's where this town gets made.
That's exactly it. Come on Thursday and say it again to the parents at the library; they need to hear it from somebody who isn't me.
I hear you on English, I teach it all day. I'd only ask you not to make the kids choose. They can carry two things.
I understand wanting to keep what we built safe. I just think the hall is safer with more friends outside it, not fewer.
Listening is allowed. When you've made up your mind, come and find me at the notice board. There's always a job.
Thank you for standing up there. Both halves of this town could use more people who'll do that.
